solution:
The aeroplane starts from rest, so \(u = 0\), and covers \(s = 500\ \text{m}\) in \(t = 30\ \text{s}\) with uniform acceleration.

Using \(s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^{2}\),

\(500 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\,a\,(30)^{2} = 450\,a\)

\(\therefore a = \dfrac{500}{450} = \dfrac{10}{9} = 1.11\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

The take-off velocity is the velocity at \(t = 30\ \text{s}\):

\(v = u + at = 0 + \dfrac{10}{9}\times 30 = \dfrac{100}{3}\)

Check: for uniform acceleration from rest the average velocity is \(\dfrac{s}{t} = \dfrac{500}{30} = 16.67\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), and \(v = 2\times 16.67 = 33.33\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), which agrees.

Velocity at take off \(= 33.33\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) (about \(120\ \text{km/hr}\)).

Convert the initial speed to SI units:

\(u = 120\ \text{km/hr} = 120\times\dfrac{5}{18} = \dfrac{100}{3} = 33.33\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

The car stops, so \(v = 0\), and \(s = 100\ \text{m}\).

(i) Average retardation, from \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\):

\(0 = (33.33)^{2} + 2a(100)\)

\(a = -\dfrac{1111.11}{200} = -5.56\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

The negative sign shows the acceleration opposes the motion, so the magnitude of the retardation is \(5.56\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

(ii) Time to stop, from \(v = u + at\):

\(0 = 33.33 - 5.56\,t\)

\(t = \dfrac{33.33}{5.56} = 6\ \text{s}\)

Check: \(s = \dfrac{u + v}{2}\,t = \dfrac{33.33}{2}\times 6 = 100\ \text{m}\), as given.

Average retardation \(= 5.56\ \text{m s}^{-2}\); time taken to come to rest \(= 6\ \text{s}\).

Average speed is the total path length divided by the total time, not the mean of the three speeds.

Convert each interval to hours and find its distance \(= \text{speed}\times\text{time}\):

\(s_{1} = 50\times\dfrac{30}{60} = 25\ \text{km}\)

\(s_{2} = 30\times\dfrac{15}{60} = 7.5\ \text{km}\)

\(s_{3} = 70\times\dfrac{45}{60} = 52.5\ \text{km}\)

Total distance \(= 25 + 7.5 + 52.5 = 85\ \text{km}\)

Total time \(= 30 + 15 + 45 = 90\ \text{min} = 1.5\ \text{hr}\)

\(v_{\text{av}} = \dfrac{85}{1.5} = 56.67\ \text{km/hr}\)

In SI units, \(56.67\times\dfrac{5}{18} = 15.74\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

Average speed \(= 56.67\ \text{km/hr} = 15.74\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

[Textbook note: the question never says whose motion the graph describes — the word "car" first appears in the list of things to determine, not in the stem. The graph itself supplies everything the five parts need.]

Read each answer off the graph, remembering that the slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration and the area under it is the distance travelled.

(i) The graph starts at the origin O, so at \(t = 0\) the velocity is zero.

Initial speed \(= 0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) (the car starts from rest).

(ii) The highest point reached on the velocity axis is at A and along AB, where \(v = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

Maximum speed \(= 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

(iii) Zero acceleration means zero slope, i.e. the horizontal portion.

Part AB, from \(t = 3\ \text{s}\) to \(t = 6\ \text{s}\), shows zero acceleration (uniform velocity).

(iv) Constant retardation means a straight line of constant negative slope.

Part BC, from \(t = 6\ \text{s}\) to \(t = 8\ \text{s}\), shows constant retardation. Its value is \(\dfrac{0 - 20}{8 - 6} = -10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), i.e. a retardation of \(10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

(v) Distance in the first \(6\ \text{s}\) is the area of the figure OABD, made of the triangle OAE and the rectangle EABD:

Area of \(\triangle\)OAE \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 20 = 30\ \text{m}\)

Area of rectangle EABD \(= 3\times 20 = 60\ \text{m}\)

Total \(= 30 + 60 = 90\ \text{m}\)

Initial speed \(= 0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); maximum speed \(= 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); zero acceleration along AB; constant retardation along BC; distance travelled in the first \(6\ \text{s} = 90\ \text{m}\).
_note: Part (i) is answered as zero because the transcribed figure states that the first segment rises from the origin O. Worth a second look at the printed graph during the cross-check: the velocity axis carries a mark at 5, and asking for the initial speed is a slightly odd question if the answer is trivially zero, so some printings of this figure start the first segment at 5 m/s rather than at O. If the printed line does start at 5, then part (i) is 5 m/s and part (v) becomes the area of a trapezium, 0.5*(5+20)*3 + 3*20 = 97.5 m. Parts (ii), (iii) and (iv) are unaffected either way.

solution:
For a given speed of projection the horizontal range \(R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}\) is greatest when \(\sin 2\theta = 1\), i.e. \(\theta = 45^\circ\). Since the man throws to the maximum possible distance, the ball was thrown at \(45^\circ\) and

\(R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^{2}}{g} = 80\ \text{m}\)

The maximum height for the same projection is

\(H = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g} = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}45^\circ}{2g} = \dfrac{u^{2}}{2g}\times\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{u^{2}}{4g}\)

\(\therefore H = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{u^{2}}{g}\right) = \dfrac{R_{\max}}{4} = \dfrac{80}{4}\)

Note that \(H\) comes out as one quarter of the maximum range, so the answer does not depend on the value taken for \(g\).

Maximum height reached \(= 20\ \text{m}\).

Take axes along the incline (\(x\)) and perpendicular to it (\(y\)). The velocity of projection makes an angle \((\theta - \phi)\) with the incline, and gravity has components \(-g\sin\phi\) along the incline and \(-g\cos\phi\) perpendicular to it.

Initial components:

\(u_{x} = v_{0}\cos(\theta - \phi)\), \(u_{y} = v_{0}\sin(\theta - \phi)\)

Accelerations:

\(a_{x} = -g\sin\phi\), \(a_{y} = -g\cos\phi\)

The projectile lands back on the incline when its perpendicular displacement is zero:

\(0 = v_{0}\sin(\theta - \phi)\,T - \dfrac{1}{2}g\cos\phi\,T^{2}\)

\(\therefore T = \dfrac{2v_{0}\sin(\theta - \phi)}{g\cos\phi}\)

The range along the incline is the displacement along \(x\) in this time:

\(R = u_{x}T + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{x}T^{2} = v_{0}\cos(\theta - \phi)\,T - \dfrac{1}{2}g\sin\phi\,T^{2}\)

Substituting \(T\) and taking \(\dfrac{2v_{0}^{2}\sin(\theta - \phi)}{g\cos^{2}\phi}\) common,

\(R = \dfrac{2v_{0}^{2}\sin(\theta - \phi)}{g\cos^{2}\phi}\Big[\cos(\theta - \phi)\cos\phi - \sin(\theta - \phi)\sin\phi\Big]\)

The bracket is \(\cos\big((\theta - \phi) + \phi\big) = \cos\theta\). Hence

\(R = \dfrac{2v_{0}^{2}\cos\theta\,\sin(\theta - \phi)}{g\cos^{2}\phi}\)

Check: putting \(\phi = 0\) gives \(R = \dfrac{2v_{0}^{2}\cos\theta\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{v_{0}^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}\), the ordinary horizontal range, as it should.

Range along the inclined surface \(R = \dfrac{2v_{0}^{2}\cos\theta\,\sin(\theta - \phi)}{g\cos^{2}\phi}\).

Constant speed \(= 72\ \text{km/hr} = 72\times\dfrac{5}{18} = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

Time A to B \(= 4\ \text{min} = 240\ \text{s}\); halt at B \(= 20\ \text{s}\); time B to C \(= 3\ \text{min} = 180\ \text{s}\). Each journey has a \(10\ \text{s}\) acceleration at the start and a \(10\ \text{s}\) retardation at the end.

(i) Velocity-time graph. Plot time (s) along the horizontal axis and velocity (\(\text{m s}^{-1}\)) along the vertical axis. The graph is a straight-line figure through the following points, joined in order:

\((0,\,0) \to (10,\,20)\): straight line rising, acceleration \(2\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

\((10,\,20) \to (230,\,20)\): horizontal line, constant speed

\((230,\,20) \to (240,\,0)\): straight line falling, retardation \(2\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), train at B

\((240,\,0) \to (260,\,0)\): along the time axis, the \(20\ \text{s}\) halt at B

\((260,\,0) \to (270,\,20)\): straight line rising

\((270,\,20) \to (430,\,20)\): horizontal line, constant speed

\((430,\,20) \to (440,\,0)\): straight line falling, train at C

The shape is therefore two trapezia separated by a \(20\ \text{s}\) gap on the time axis.

(ii) Distance = area under the graph.

Station A to B: the trapezium has parallel sides \(240\ \text{s}\) (total time) and \(240 - 10 - 10 = 220\ \text{s}\) (time at constant speed), and height \(20\ \text{m s}^{-1}\):

\(s_{AB} = \dfrac{1}{2}(240 + 220)\times 20 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 460\times 20 = 4600\ \text{m} = 4.6\ \text{km}\)

Station B to C: parallel sides \(180\ \text{s}\) and \(180 - 10 - 10 = 160\ \text{s}\):

\(s_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{2}(180 + 160)\times 20 = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 340\times 20 = 3400\ \text{m} = 3.4\ \text{km}\)

Total distance A to C \(= 4600 + 3400 = 8000\ \text{m} = 8\ \text{km}\)

Distance A to B \(= 4600\ \text{m} = 4.6\ \text{km}\); distance B to C \(= 3400\ \text{m} = 3.4\ \text{km}\); distance A to C \(= 8000\ \text{m} = 8\ \text{km}\).
diagramNote: Part (i) asks the student to plot a velocity-time graph. A figure would show the two trapezia through (0,0), (10,20), (230,20), (240,0), the flat halt from (240,0) to (260,0), then (270,20), (430,20) and (440,0), with time (s) on the x-axis and velocity (m/s) on the y-axis.

solution:
Take east along \(\hat{i}\) and north along \(\hat{j}\). Add the velocities in stages, using \(\vec{v}_{\text{fly, Earth}} = \vec{v}_{\text{fly, waiter}} + \vec{v}_{\text{waiter, train}} + \vec{v}_{\text{train, Earth}}\).

\(\vec{v}_{\text{train, Earth}} = 10\,\hat{i}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\vec{v}_{\text{waiter, train}} = 1.2\,\hat{i}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\vec{v}_{\text{fly, waiter}} = 2\,\hat{j}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore \vec{v}_{\text{fly, Earth}} = (10 + 1.2)\,\hat{i} + 2\,\hat{j} = 11.2\,\hat{i} + 2\,\hat{j}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

Magnitude:

\(v = \sqrt{(11.2)^{2} + (2)^{2}} = \sqrt{125.44 + 4} = \sqrt{129.44} = 11.38\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

Direction, measured north of east:

\(\tan\alpha = \dfrac{2}{11.2} = 0.1786\)

\(\alpha = \tan^{-1}(0.1786) = 10.1^\circ\)

Velocity of the fly relative to the Earth \(= 11.2\,\hat{i} + 2\,\hat{j}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), i.e. \(11.38\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) directed \(10.1^\circ\) north of east.

The speed is constant, so the only acceleration is the centripetal acceleration \(a = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r}\), directed towards the centre.

First find the radius. In one revolution the car covers the circumference in the period \(T = 40\ \text{s}\):

\(2\pi r = vT = 50\times 40 = 2000\ \text{m}\)

\(r = \dfrac{2000}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1000}{\pi} = 318.3\ \text{m}\)

Therefore

\(a = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{(50)^{2}}{318.3} = \dfrac{2500}{318.3} = 7.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

Equivalently, \(a = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{2\pi v}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi\times 50}{40} = 7.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

Magnitude of the acceleration \(= 7.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), directed towards the centre of the circle.

For uniform circular motion the centripetal acceleration is

\(a = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r}\)

Given \(v = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(r = 2\ \text{m}\),

\(a = \dfrac{(15)^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{225}{2}\)

Centripetal acceleration \(= 112.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), directed along the radius towards the centre of the circle.

The horizontal range is \(R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}\), with \(\theta = 30^\circ\) and \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

\(\sin 2\theta = \sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.866\)

\(\therefore R = \dfrac{u^{2}(0.866)}{10}\), so \(u = \sqrt{\dfrac{Rg}{\sin 60^\circ}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10R}{0.866}}\)

Since \(R\) increases with \(u\), the two limits of \(R\) give the two limits of \(u\).

For \(R = 40\ \text{m}\):

\(u^{2} = \dfrac{40\times 10}{0.866} = 461.9\), \(u = 21.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

For \(R = 50\ \text{m}\):

\(u^{2} = \dfrac{50\times 10}{0.866} = 577.4\), \(u = 24.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

The initial velocity must lie between \(21.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(24.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).
